item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of October 19 - October 26, 2026
item.description:
# QE ArXiv Watch Weekly Week ending October 26, 2026

This week’s useful reminder: getting to an answer sooner is only a win if we know what risk we’re taking to get there. Two papers tackle that trade-off in online experiments from different angles—and a reliability study shows why a “best” maintenance age can be much less certain than its cost estimate suggests.

Faster A/B tests, with the guardrails made explicit. Perini et al. build group sequential designs that can stop an experiment early while retaining the platform’s fixed-horizon terminal decision rule. Their predictive-probability stopping policy cut expected duration by 41.7% in simulation; online experiments showed a 43.1% runtime reduction and an estimated 76% increase in testing capacity. The practical appeal is clear: less waiting without quietly loosening error-rate or power targets. But the policy’s boundaries and horizon are chosen by simulation, so teams should validate them against their own traffic patterns and outcome correlations.

Lu et al. address a different trap: repeatedly checking a clustered experiment’s quantile results. Their CAQ method provides sequential confidence sequences for quantile effects when users contribute multiple correlated events. In simulations, cumulative miscoverage stayed around 3%, while “peek at a fixed-horizon test” and “ignore clustering” baselines failed badly. CAQ’s validity is asymptotic, not an exact finite-sample guarantee; still, it’s a promising option when tail behavior matters and experiments are monitored continuously.

Maintenance decisions need risk ranges, not just a point estimate. Wu et al. model changing inter-failure times with a geometric process and quantify uncertainty in both reliability and replacement age. In an aircraft example with just 27 intervals, two strategies at cycle 9 had cost rates of 12.705 and 13.767—but reliabilities of 0.912 and 0.670. That’s a striking reminder that modest expected-cost differences can conceal substantial risk differences. Their generalized confidence intervals had better coverage than bootstrap and Bayesian intervals in several small-sample simulations. For practitioners, the message is to show decision-makers the reliability consequences of a replacement policy, not only its average cost.

A useful counterpoint to this week’s enthusiasm for adaptive methods comes from Nyaupane et al., who audit learned experimental-design controllers. In one simulated voltage-clamp task, policies presented as learned feedback controllers always chose the same protocol; masking the observed current changed nothing. In a task where the best next pulse truly depended on the first observation, they did adapt—and matched a Bayesian reference. Clever algorithms can use feedback, but we should test whether the feedback actually changes decisions and improves outcomes.

The remaining papers focus on getting the design right for messy experiments. Zhang et al. show how rerandomization and Lasso adjustment can sharpen network-effect estimates, while accounting for auxiliary variables that themselves depend on assignment. Singh et al. tackle therapist capacity, availability, and turnover: flexible allocation can substantially reduce the number of batches needed, though no strategy dominates across settings. And Kaji et al. offer a two-stage design for multi-arm trials with noncompliance, identifying a targeted local effect under specific assumptions about treatment choice and receipt.

Across the week, the common thread is operational realism: clustering, interference, scarce staff, noncompliance, changing failure rates. The question for us is not simply whether a method is adaptive or efficient. It’s whether its assumptions match the system we’re trying to improve.

Featured Papers This Week

  • Wu et al.: Finite-horizon maintenance under geometric-process models: Quantifying model and decision uncertainty (Reliability)
  • Lu et al.: CAQ: Clustered Asymptotically Anytime-Valid Quantile Treatment Effects for Online Experiments (DOE)
  • Perini et al.: Let Them Peek: Group Sequential Designs for A/B Testing (DOE)
  • Zhang et al.: Rerandomization and high-dimensional adjustment with assignment-dependent auxiliary variables under network interference (DOE)
  • Nyaupane et al.: When Does Feedback Help? Auditing Learned Voltage-Clamp Experimental Design (DOE)
  • Singh et al.: Incorporating therapist capacity, availability and turnover in trials of therapist-delivered interventions: Non-orthogonal factorial designs (DOE)
  • Kaji et al.: A LATE-Targeting Experimental Design for Multi-Arm RCTs (DOE)
